questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus reports 1 year of erections insufficient for intercourse despite intact desire. He also notes fewer morning erections. Oral first-line therapy is prescribed. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agonism of central melanocortin receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of neuronal sodium channel conduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of nitric oxide synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of serotonin reuptake at spinal synapses

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of the enzyme that degrades cGMP

explanation.summary: PDE5 inhibitors are first-line for erectile dysfunction and work by blocking cGMP breakdown.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-line treatment for erectile dysfunction is an oral PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil). PDE5 normally metabolizes cGMP; inhibiting it prolongs NO-mediated cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation, arterial inflow, and venous trapping, enhancing the erectile response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Melanocortin receptor agonism is the mechanism of bremelanotide, used for female sexual interest/arousal disorder, not erectile dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sodium channel blockade describes local anesthetics such as lidocaine, used topically for premature ejaculation or penetration-related pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PDE5 inhibitors do not generate nitric oxide; they preserve cGMP downstream, which is why benefit requires some retained capacity to produce endothelial and neurogenic NO.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased serotonergic signaling (SSRIs) inhibits arousal reflexes and delays ejaculation; it treats premature ejaculation and can cause erectile dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man sustains a complete spinal cord transection at the T4 level in a motorcycle collision. Several months later, he is still able to achieve erections with direct genital stimulation. Which of the following pathways most likely mediates this preserved response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cortical arousal centers via descending spinal tracts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypothalamic nuclei via brainstem autonomic relays

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sacral parasympathetic neurons via the pelvic splanchnic nerves

choices.label: D
choices.text: Somatic motor neurons via the pudendal nerve

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thoracolumbar sympathetic neurons via the hypogastric nerve

explanation.summary: Reflexogenic erections are mediated by a sacral (S2-S4) parasympathetic reflex arc that does not require input from the brain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sacral parasympathetic neurons (S2-S4) mediate reflexogenic arousal from direct genital stimulation, controlling vasodilation and engorgement of erectile tissue via the pelvic splanchnic nerves. Because this reflex arc is entirely below a T4 lesion, males with severed spinal cords can still achieve erections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Descending cortical input is interrupted by a complete T4 transection, so brain-initiated (psychogenic) pathways cannot explain the preserved response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypothalamic and brainstem pathways also require intact descending spinal connections, which a complete T4 lesion eliminates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic motor neurons via the pudendal nerve drive rhythmic bulbocavernosus and ischiocavernosus contractions during orgasm and expulsion, not erection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thoracolumbar sympathetic neurons (T11-L2) mediate psychogenic arousal and the emission phase of ejaculation, not the reflex erection from genital touch.

questions.stem: During the male sexual response, sperm move from the epididymis through the ductus deferens, and the prostate and seminal vesicles contract to push their contents into the bulb of the urethra, after which ejaculation can no longer be voluntarily stopped. Which of the following controls this phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibitory GABAergic outflow from brainstem nuclei

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nonadrenergic-noncholinergic nerve terminal signaling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sacral parasympathetic outflow through pelvic splanchnic nerves

choices.label: D
choices.text: Somatic motor outflow through the pudendal nerve

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sympathetic outflow from thoracolumbar spinal segments

explanation.summary: Emission is under sympathetic control from thoracolumbar (T11-L2) neurons traveling via the hypogastric nerve.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sympathetic stimulation causes the ductus deferens, prostate, and seminal vesicles to contract, pushing contents into the urethral bulb. Thoracolumbar sympathetic neurons (T11-L2) control the emission phase of ejaculation, with efferent fibers in the hypogastric nerve.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GABA provides inhibition in brain and spinal circuits; it dampens rather than executes the emission reflex.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NANC terminals release nitric oxide for smooth muscle relaxation and erection, the opposite of the contractile events of emission.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parasympathetic stimulation increases glandular secretions during excitement and plateau and mediates erection; it does not drive emission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pudendal nerve carries somatic fibers for the expulsion phase, the rhythmic ischiocavernosus and bulbocavernosus contractions that expel semen.

questions.stem: Researchers studying the human sexual response want a reliable neuroendocrine marker that orgasm has occurred in study participants of either sex. A blood level of which of the following hormones is best suited for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estradiol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxytocin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progesterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolactin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone

explanation.summary: Prolactin rises substantially after orgasm in both sexes and stays elevated for over an hour, making it a reliable orgasm marker.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prolactin demonstrates a substantial, long-lasting increase following orgasm in both males and females, rising immediately and remaining elevated for 60 or more minutes. This sustained rise makes it a reliable neuroendocrine marker of orgasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estradiol positively predicts sexual desire across the cycle in naturally cycling females; it is not a post-orgasm marker.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxytocin does increase acutely after orgasm, but its changes are less consistent and less sustained than prolactin elevations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Progesterone negatively predicts sexual desire in naturally cycling females and does not mark the occurrence of orgasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testosterone supports desire, arousal, and erectile function but is not described as spiking reliably after orgasm.

questions.stem: A study tracks daily hormone levels and self-reported sexual desire in healthy, naturally cycling women who are not using hormonal contraception. Based on the known hormonal influences on female sexual function, which pattern of results is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desire falls with both higher estradiol and higher progesterone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desire rises with both higher estradiol and higher progesterone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desire rises with higher estradiol and falls with higher progesterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Desire rises with higher progesterone and falls with higher estradiol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Desire tracks prolactin levels and ignores ovarian steroids

explanation.summary: In naturally cycling females, estradiol positively predicts sexual desire while progesterone negatively predicts it.
explanation.whyCorrect: In naturally cycling females, estradiol positively predicts sexual desire and progesterone negatively predicts sexual desire, so desire should be highest when estradiol is high and progesterone is low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estradiol positively predicts desire, so desire should not fall as estradiol rises.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Progesterone negatively predicts desire, so desire should not rise with rising progesterone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses both relationships: progesterone is the negative predictor and estradiol the positive one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolactin is a post-orgasm marker; ovarian steroids, not prolactin, are the predictors of cycling desire described.

questions.stem: During penile erection, intracavernosal pressure rises to approximate systolic blood pressure even before the ischiocavernosus muscles contract. Which of the following mechanisms is most responsible for trapping blood within the corpora cavernosa at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Closure of the bladder neck by sympathetic stimulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compression of the subtunical venous plexus against the tunica albuginea

choices.label: C
choices.text: Constriction of cavernosal arteries reducing arterial inflow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Contraction of trabecular smooth muscle within the sinusoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thickening and tightening of the scrotum around the testes

explanation.summary: The veno-occlusive mechanism traps blood when expanding sinusoids compress subtunical veins against the rigid tunica albuginea.
explanation.whyCorrect: As the erectile bodies engorge, expanded sinusoids compress the subtunical venous plexus against the rigid tunica albuginea, restricting venous outflow and raising intracavernosal pressure to approximately systolic pressure. Ischiocavernosus contraction under pudendal control then pushes pressure above systolic for full rigidity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bladder neck closure occurs during ejaculation to prevent semen from mixing with urine; it does not trap blood in the corpora.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erection depends on increased arterial inflow through dilated arteries; arterial constriction would oppose erection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erection requires relaxation, not contraction, of trabecular smooth muscle so arterial blood can fill the sinusoidal spaces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scrotal thickening and testicular elevation are plateau-phase changes and do not restrict penile venous outflow.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman asks her physician about a small volume of thick, milky fluid she sometimes releases at orgasm, which she distinguishes from her usual lubrication during arousal. This fluid most likely originates from which of the following structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bulbourethral gland homologue secreting mucus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clitoral corpora cavernosa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paraurethral (Skene's) glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uterine smooth muscle glands

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaginal capillary transudation

explanation.summary: True female ejaculate is a small volume of thick, milky, PSA-containing fluid from the paraurethral (Skene's) glands.
explanation.whyCorrect: True female ejaculation originates from the paraurethral (Skene's) glands, the embryologic homologue of the male prostate. The fluid is a few milliliters of thick, milky secretion containing prostate-specific antigen and prostatic acid phosphatase, and may protect the urethra from microbes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Skene's glands are the homologue of the prostate, not of the bulbourethral glands, and the fluid is milky and PSA-rich rather than lubricating mucus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The clitoral corpora cavernosa are erectile vascular tissue that engorges; they are not secretory glands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The uterus contracts during orgasm but is not the source of the milky ejaculate described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaginal lubrication is a neurogenic plasma transudate driven by capillary pressure during vasocongestion; it is distinctly different from female ejaculation.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman reports that for the past 8 months she has had no interest in sexual activity, no erotic thoughts, no excitement or pleasure during encounters, and no arousal in response to cues she previously found stimulating. She is tearful and says the change is straining her marriage. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A daily trial of a serotonergic antidepressant such as an SSRI

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily oral flibanserin taken at bedtime each night

choices.label: C
choices.text: Off-label transdermal testosterone replacement therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Psychological interventions such as CBT and couples therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subcutaneous bremelanotide before anticipated sexual activity

explanation.summary: Female sexual interest/arousal disorder is treated first with psychological interventions; medications are second options.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient meets criteria for FSIAD: at least 3 of the 6 indicators are absent for at least 6 months with clinically significant distress. Psychological interventions, including CBT, mindfulness-based therapy, and couples or sex therapy, are first line for FSIAD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SSRIs increase serotonergic signaling, which inhibits arousal reflexes; they cause rather than treat low desire and arousal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flibanserin, which is thought to alter central serotonergic signaling, is a medication option but not first-line therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Testosterone is off-label in the US, with the strongest evidence limited to carefully selected postmenopausal patients, and is not first line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bremelanotide, a melanocortin receptor agonist, is likewise a medication option rather than the initial treatment.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman reports 9 months of marked vulvar pain with attempted vaginal penetration, intense anxiety in anticipation of intercourse, and involuntary tightening of the muscles around the vaginal opening. The symptoms cause significant distress. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An SNRI for pain modulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily oral gabapentin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pelvic floor physical therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical local anesthetic before intercourse

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical vaginal estrogen

explanation.summary: Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder is treated first with pelvic floor physical therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: She meets criteria for GPPPD, the DSM-5 diagnosis combining dyspareunia and vaginismus: over 6 months of penetration difficulty, pelvic pain, fear or anxiety about pain, and pelvic floor tensing with distress. Pelvic floor physical therapy is first line because it directly targets the neuromuscular dysfunction with biofeedback, manual therapy, relaxation training, and graded dilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SNRIs can reduce centralized or neuropathic pelvic pain but are a medication option rather than first-line management.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gabapentin, which dampens neuronal excitability via voltage-activated calcium channels, is an etiology-dependent medication option, not initial therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Local anesthetics reduce peripheral pain signaling during penetration but do not address the underlying pelvic floor dysfunction and are not first line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaginal estrogen is most useful for hypoestrogenic or atrophy-related dyspareunia, which this young patient's presentation does not suggest.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is distressed because he consistently ejaculates within about a minute of penetration and cannot delay it, which is straining his relationship. Along with behavioral techniques, pharmacotherapy is planned. Which of the following best explains why the first-line drug class is effective for this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced dopaminergic signaling heightens sexual desire

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased serotonergic signaling inhibits the ejaculatory reflex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Melanocortin receptor agonism modulates central arousal pathways

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preserved cGMP prolongs cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced catecholamine reuptake increases noradrenergic tone

explanation.summary: SSRIs are first-line for premature ejaculation because serotonin inhibits the ejaculatory reflex and delays ejaculation.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is premature ejaculation: ejaculation within about 1 minute of penetration with inability to delay it and significant distress. SSRIs, including on-demand dapoxetine, are first-line medications because increased serotonergic signaling inhibits the ejaculatory reflex; topical anesthetics are also first line, and combination therapy beats monotherapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dopamine facilitates desire and arousal; enhancing it would not delay ejaculation and is not the treatment mechanism here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Melanocortin agonism describes bremelanotide, used for female sexual interest/arousal disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: cGMP preservation is the PDE5 inhibitor mechanism used for erectile dysfunction, not for delaying ejaculation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibition describes bupropion, used to improve desire or counter SSRI-related dysfunction, not to delay ejaculation.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department with a painful erection that has lasted 6 hours. He recently started taking trazodone for insomnia. In addition to corporal aspiration, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collagenase injection into the corpora

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intracavernosal phenylephrine injection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Observation until detumescence occurs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral sildenafil administration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical lidocaine application

explanation.summary: Ischemic priapism is a medical emergency treated with corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: A sustained, painful erection lasting longer than 4 hours is priapism, which is associated with sickle cell disease and with medications, trazodone being among the most common. Ischemic priapism requires immediate treatment to prevent permanent tissue damage and erectile dysfunction; common treatments are corporal aspiration to drain excess blood and intracavernosal phenylephrine to open veins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Collagenase is used to break down the fibrous plaques of Peyronie disease, not to treat priapism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ischemic priapism is a medical emergency; observation risks permanent tissue damage and erectile dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sildenafil prolongs smooth muscle relaxation and enhances erection, which would worsen rather than relieve priapism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical lidocaine reduces sensory pain signaling but does nothing to relieve the trapped blood causing ischemia.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus is evaluated for infertility. He reports normal orgasms but says little or no semen comes out, and his urine appears cloudy after intercourse. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lax sphincter at the base of the bladder

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of the seminal vesicles to produce fructose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrous plaques surrounding the corpora cavernosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of the ductus deferens by scarring

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weakness of the bulbocavernosus and ischiocavernosus muscles

explanation.summary: Retrograde ejaculation, a cause of male infertility, usually results from a lax bladder-neck sphincter, commonly from diabetes, pelvic surgery, or autonomic dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: During normal ejaculation the bladder neck closes tightly so semen cannot mix with urine. Retrograde ejaculation occurs when this sphincter is lax, letting semen pass backward into the bladder; common causes include diabetes mellitus, prostate or other pelvic surgery, autonomic nerve dysfunction, and certain antidepressants and antipsychotics.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Seminal vesicle fructose supplies sperm energy; its absence would not send semen backward into the bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrous plaques around the corpora cavernosa cause Peyronie disease, with penile curvature and painful erections, not absent antegrade semen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ductal obstruction is not the mechanism described for this diabetes-associated pattern of orgasm with semen appearing in the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weak striated pelvic muscles would impair expulsion force but would not divert semen into the bladder or cloud the post-coital urine.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old female reports 8 months of menstrual cycles that have become progressively lighter and farther apart, along with new nighttime episodes of sudden warmth, flushing, and sweating that wake her from sleep. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following best characterizes her current reproductive state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Menopause, because vasomotor symptoms have begun

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perimenopause, the transition preceding the final menstrual period

choices.label: C
choices.text: Postmenopause, because her cycles are lighter than baseline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Premature ovarian insufficiency, because she is younger than 51

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary amenorrhea, because her cycle length has increased

explanation.summary: Irregular, spaced-out cycles with new vasomotor symptoms in the 40s define perimenopause; menopause requires 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Perimenopause is the interval of years before the final menstrual period marked by fluctuating hormone levels, irregular cycles, and the onset of vasomotor symptoms, typically beginning in the 40s or 50s and lasting 2-8 years. Because this patient is still menstruating, she has not met the diagnostic criterion for menopause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea, not by the onset of hot flashes; she menstruated 6 weeks ago.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Postmenopause refers to the years after menopause has occurred; she has not yet reached menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Onset of the menopausal transition in the late 40s is typical, not premature; the average age of menopause is 51, with 90% between 45 and 56.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She continues to menstruate, so she does not have amenorrhea; her irregular cycles reflect the normal menopausal transition.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old female with 14 months of amenorrhea undergoes laboratory testing. Her physician notes that one hormonal change is considered the primary indicator of menopause. An increase in which of the following, driven by loss of a specific ovarian follicular product, best fits this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrone, due to peripheral aromatization of androgens

choices.label: B
choices.text: FSH, due to decreased inhibin B production

choices.label: C
choices.text: GnRH, due to loss of progesterone negative feedback

choices.label: D
choices.text: LH, due to loss of estrogen negative feedback

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolactin, due to loss of dopaminergic inhibition

explanation.summary: The primary hormonal change indicating menopause is a marked rise in FSH, driven by decreased inhibin B production from ovarian follicles.
explanation.whyCorrect: With loss of ovarian follicular activity, follicles no longer produce inhibin B, releasing FSH from its selective negative feedback. FSH therefore rises markedly and is the primary hormonal indicator of menopause, alongside decreased estrogen and progesterone and increased LH and GnRH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ovarian estrogen production falls in menopause; a rise in estrogen is not the hormonal marker of menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GnRH rises, but it is not singled out as the primary indicator, and inhibin B loss specifically drives FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LH does rise in menopause, but the lecture identifies the FSH increase, driven by lost inhibin B, as the primary indicator.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolactin is not part of the hormonal profile of menopause described in this lecture.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female who reached menopause at age 51 presents with two episodes of light vaginal spotting over the past month. She takes no hormone therapy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial atrophy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endometrial cancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endometrial polyp

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resumption of ovulation

explanation.summary: Endometrial atrophy is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Postmenopausal bleeding is most commonly caused by endometrial atrophy; other causes include endometrial polyps and hormone replacement therapy. Only approximately 10% of postmenopausal bleeding is caused by endometrial cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infection is not among the leading causes of postmenopausal bleeding taught here; atrophy remains most likely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endometrial cancer accounts for only about 10% of postmenopausal bleeding; it must be considered but is not the most likely cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endometrial polyps cause postmenopausal bleeding but are less common than atrophy as the etiology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Menopause is a permanent cessation of menses from loss of ovarian follicular activity; ovulation does not resume 9 years later.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old female with an intact uterus has severe hot flashes and night sweats that have not improved with lifestyle changes. She and her physician decide to start systemic estrogen therapy. Adding a progestogen to her regimen is necessary primarily to reduce the risk of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasive breast cancer and recurrence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ischemic stroke and coronary events

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrent urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: In a female with an intact uterus, a progestogen must accompany systemic estrogen to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from unopposed estrogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unopposed systemic estrogen stimulates the endometrium and can cause endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Combined estrogen-progestogen therapy is therefore required for females with an intact uterus, whereas females who have had a hysterectomy can use estrogen-only therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: VTE is a risk of hormone therapy itself, mitigated by transdermal rather than oral routes, not by adding a progestogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breast cancer risk was increased in the WHI combined estrogen-progestogen arm; progestogen does not protect against it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stroke is a risk of hormone therapy (seen even in the estrogen-only WHI arm); progestogen does not prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Estrogen therapy decreases UTI risk; UTI prevention is not the purpose of the progestogen.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old female with moderate vasomotor symptoms is choosing between oral and transdermal estradiol. Her physician explains that the transdermal route carries lower risks of venous thromboembolism and stroke. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen acts as a receptor antagonist in the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen is absorbed only by urogenital tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen is converted to progesterone in the skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transdermal estrogen raises sex hormone-binding globulin levels

explanation.summary: Transdermal estrogens avoid first-pass hepatic metabolism, so they do not increase hepatic production of clotting factors the way oral estrogens do.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oral estrogens undergo first-pass hepatic metabolism, which increases production of clotting factors, inflammatory markers, and sex hormone-binding globulin. Transdermal patches, gels, and sprays bypass this first pass, producing more stable hormone levels and lower risks of venous thromboembolism and stroke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transdermal estrogen is not a hepatic receptor antagonist; tissue-selective agonist/antagonist activity describes SERMs like ospemifene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delivery limited to urogenital tissue describes low-dose vaginal estrogen, not systemic transdermal therapy, which treats vasomotor symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estrogen is not converted to progesterone in the skin; this is not a described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raising SHBG is an effect of oral estrogen's first-pass metabolism, the very effect transdermal dosing avoids.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old female with an intact uterus reports vaginal dryness, pain with intercourse, and two urinary tract infections in the past year. She denies hot flashes or night sweats. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-dose local estrogen therapy without a progestogen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral conjugated equine estrogens with a progestogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral gabapentin at bedtime

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral paroxetine at bedtime

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transdermal estradiol patch with a progestogen

explanation.summary: Isolated genitourinary symptoms are best treated with low-dose vaginal estrogen, which needs no progestogen even with an intact uterus.
explanation.whyCorrect: For females with primarily genitourinary symptoms and no significant vasomotor symptoms, low-dose vaginal estrogen is preferred. Creams, tablets, and rings deliver estrogen directly to urogenital tissue with minimal systemic absorption, treating dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent UTIs, and the minimal endometrial exposure means no concurrent progestogen is required.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Systemic oral estrogen adds thromboembolic and other systemic risks she does not need, since she has no vasomotor symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gabapentin helps hot flashes and night sweats, not vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, or recurrent UTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paroxetine targets vasomotor symptoms, which she does not have, and does not treat atrophic genitourinary changes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Systemic transdermal therapy is likewise unnecessary for purely genitourinary symptoms that local therapy treats effectively.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old female with a history of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, now in remission, has frequent daytime hot flashes. She asks about medication options. Which of the following is FDA-approved specifically for menopausal hot flashes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Citalopram

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desvenlafaxine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escitalopram

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paroxetine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venlafaxine

explanation.summary: Paroxetine is the SSRI that is FDA-approved for menopausal hot flashes; hormone therapy is contraindicated with current or hormone-sensitive cancer history.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hormone-sensitive breast cancer is a contraindication to hormone replacement therapy, so a non-hormonal agent is appropriate. Among SSRIs/SNRIs used for vasomotor symptoms, paroxetine is specifically FDA-approved for menopausal hot flashes; the class reduces hot flash frequency by roughly 40-60%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Citalopram has shown benefit in trials but is not FDA-approved for hot flashes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desvenlafaxine has trial evidence of benefit but is not the FDA-approved agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Escitalopram has trial evidence of benefit but lacks FDA approval for hot flashes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venlafaxine has shown benefit in clinical trials but is not FDA-approved for this indication.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female has drenching night sweats that repeatedly wake her, and she cannot fall back asleep afterward. She declines hormone therapy. Which non-hormonal medication, taken at bedtime, is particularly well suited to her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gabapentin, via calcium channel modulation and sedation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ospemifene, via estrogen agonism in vaginal tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxybutynin, via inhibition of sweat gland activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paroxetine, via serotonin reuptake inhibition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venlafaxine, via norepinephrine reuptake inhibition

explanation.summary: Gabapentin's sedating properties make it especially useful for night sweats with sleep disturbance when dosed at bedtime.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gabapentin is an anticonvulsant that modulates calcium channels and affects thermoregulation, reducing hot flashes by approximately 50%. Its sedating effect, ordinarily a side effect, becomes an advantage for females whose vasomotor symptoms are concentrated at night and disrupt sleep.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ospemifene treats dyspareunia from vulvovaginal atrophy; it has no role in vasomotor symptoms or sleep.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin has efficacy for hot flashes but offers no sleep benefit, and anticholinergic effects limit its use in older females.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paroxetine helps vasomotor symptoms but is not highlighted for bedtime dosing to aid sleep the way gabapentin is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venlafaxine reduces hot flashes but is not the sedating bedtime option suited to nighttime symptoms.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old female with painful intercourse due to vulvovaginal atrophy prefers an oral medication over vaginal preparations. Her physician prescribes ospemifene. Which of the following best describes this drug's mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticholinergic inhibitor of glandular secretion in the vagina and vulva

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aromatase inhibitor that raises local estradiol concentrations in the vagina

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen receptor agonist in vaginal tissue, neutral or antagonist elsewhere

choices.label: D
choices.text: Estrogen receptor antagonist in vaginal tissue, agonist in bone and the uterus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progesterone receptor agonist acting on the endometrium and myometrium

explanation.summary: Ospemifene is an oral SERM that acts as an estrogen agonist in vaginal tissue while remaining neutral or antagonist in other tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ospemifene is an oral selective estrogen receptor modulator approved for dyspareunia associated with vulvovaginal atrophy. Its tissue selectivity, agonist activity in vaginal tissue with neutral or antagonist effects elsewhere, allows it to treat atrophic symptoms without generalized estrogenic stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergic inhibition of glands describes oxybutynin's effect on sweat glands, not ospemifene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It does not inhibit aromatase; aromatase inhibition would lower, not exploit, estrogenic signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its agonist activity is in vaginal tissue; it is not a vaginal antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It modulates estrogen receptors, not progesterone receptors, and is not endometrium-targeted therapy.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old female, 12 years postmenopausal, is found to have low bone mineral density on screening. Which of the following cellular changes best explains the accelerated bone loss that follows menopause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased osteoclast activity with increased osteoblast activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased osteocyte density with increased mineralization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased osteoblast activity with normal osteoclast activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased osteoclast activity with decreased osteoblast activity

explanation.summary: Estrogen loss after menopause increases osteoclast activity and decreases osteoblast activity, producing osteoporosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Declining estrogen removes its restraint on bone resorption: osteoclast activity increases while osteoblast activity decreases, tipping remodeling toward net bone loss. This is why postmenopausal females are at elevated risk of osteoporosis, and why HRT produces significant fracture reduction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This pattern would build bone rather than lose it, the opposite of postmenopausal physiology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Changes in mineralization density are not the mechanism taught; the imbalance is between osteoclasts and osteoblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Growth plates are closed in adults; chondrocyte proliferation is irrelevant to postmenopausal bone loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoblast activity falls, not rises, after estrogen loss, and osteoclast activity is increased.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male reports several years of slowly worsening fatigue, reduced libido, and fewer morning erections. His physician explains how age-related testosterone decline differs from menopause. Which of the following statements best captures that difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Testosterone ceases abruptly once Leydig cell activity is lost at a set age

choices.label: B
choices.text: Testosterone decline arises only from failure of hypothalamic GnRH output

choices.label: C
choices.text: Testosterone decline is diagnosed after 12 months of absent morning erections

choices.label: D
choices.text: Testosterone decline spares free testosterone because SHBG falls with age

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone declines gradually at about 1% per year without defined stages

explanation.summary: Unlike menopause, andropause is a gradual, stage-less decline in testosterone of roughly 1% per year beginning around age 40.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beginning around age 40, testosterone falls about 1% per year, with the decline more pronounced in free testosterone because of alterations in sex hormone-binding globulin. In contrast to menopause, andropause has a gradual onset and slow progression without defined stages, and it results from both central (hypothalamic-pituitary) and peripheral (Leydig cell responsiveness) mechanisms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no abrupt cessation at a set age; abrupt loss of gonadal hormone output is the pattern of menopause, not andropause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The decline is both central (decreased hypothalamic-pituitary function) and peripheral (reduced Leydig cell responsiveness), not purely central.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No 12-month diagnostic criterion exists for andropause; that retrospective rule defines menopause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Free testosterone falls more, not less, because of SHBG alterations with age.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old male with symptomatic hypogonadism confirmed by low serum testosterone begins intramuscular testosterone replacement therapy. Three months later his testosterone level is 950 ng/dL. Continuing this dose places him at increased risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cardiovascular complications and suppressed spermatogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed hormone exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hot flashes from hypothalamic thermoregulatory dysfunction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osteoporosis and progressive loss of muscle mass

choices.label: E
choices.text: Worsening erectile dysfunction and reduced libido

explanation.summary: Testosterone replacement should target the physiologic range of 400-700 ng/dL; supratherapeutic levels raise the risk of cardiovascular complications, BPH, and suppressed spermatogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The goal of testosterone replacement therapy is a level within the physiologic range of 400-700 ng/dL with symptom improvement. At 950 ng/dL this patient is supratherapeutic, which may increase the risk of cardiovascular complications, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and suppression of spermatogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Endometrial hyperplasia is a risk of unopposed estrogen in females with a uterus, not of testosterone therapy in males.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hot flashes from estrogen withdrawal are a menopausal phenomenon, not a described risk of excess testosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone and muscle loss are consequences of low testosterone, not of supratherapeutic replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erectile dysfunction and low libido are symptoms of hypogonadism that therapy aims to improve, not risks of excess dosing.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with irregular menses since menarche, worsening hirsutism of the chin and upper lip, and acne. Her BMI is 33 kg/m2. Pelvic ultrasound shows multiple peripheral ovarian follicles in a string-of-pearls pattern. Laboratory studies show an elevated free testosterone with a normal DHEA-S. Which of the following best explains her elevated free testosterone level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal 21-hydroxylase deficiency shunting precursors to androgens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autonomous DHEA-S secretion from an adrenal neoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased GnRH pulse frequency reducing FSH secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperinsulinemia suppressing sex hormone-binding globulin production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased hepatic synthesis of sex hormone-binding globulin

explanation.summary: In PCOS, insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia suppress SHBG, raising free testosterone.
explanation.whyCorrect: PCOS involves a self-reinforcing cycle in which increased GnRH pulse frequency drives LH-mediated ovarian androgen overproduction, while insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia further stimulate androgen synthesis and suppress SHBG. Lower SHBG leaves a larger fraction of testosterone unbound, so free testosterone rises.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is screened for with 17-OHP and is an adrenal cause; her normal DHEA-S and classic PCOS picture point to an ovarian etiology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An adrenal androgen source would produce an elevated DHEA-S, which is normal here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCOS features an increased, not decreased, GnRH pulse frequency, which favors LH-driven ovarian androgen production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SHBG is suppressed, not increased, in PCOS; increased SHBG would lower, not raise, free testosterone.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with 4 months of rapidly progressive facial hair growth and deepening of her voice. Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated DHEA-S, a mildly elevated total testosterone, and a normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Which of the following is the most likely source of her androgen excess?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tumor of the adrenal gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: An androgen-secreting ovarian tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: LH-driven ovarian overproduction in PCOS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surreptitious use of danazol

explanation.summary: An elevated DHEA-S localizes androgen excess to an adrenal source.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the female hyperandrogenism workup, elevated DHEA-S suggests an adrenal source, while elevated testosterone with normal DHEA-S points to an ovarian etiology. Rapid virilization with a markedly elevated DHEA-S and normal 17-OHP therefore indicates an adrenal tumor, and adrenal CT imaging is pursued when DHEA-S is elevated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An ovarian tumor such as a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor produces elevated testosterone with a normal DHEA-S.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is screened for with 17-OHP, which is normal in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PCOS causes gradual hirsutism with irregular menses, not rapid virilization with a markedly elevated DHEA-S.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exogenous agents like danazol would not produce a markedly elevated endogenous DHEA-S.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman is evaluated for hirsutism and irregular menses. As part of the initial laboratory workup for hyperandrogenism, which of the following tests screens for congenital adrenal hyperplasia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 17-hydroxyprogesterone

choices.label: B
choices.text: DHEA sulfate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free testosterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Luteinizing hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sex hormone-binding globulin

explanation.summary: 17-OHP is the screening test for congenital adrenal hyperplasia in hyperandrogenic females.
explanation.whyCorrect: Initial labs for female hyperandrogenism include total and free testosterone, DHEA-S, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone. The 17-OHP is included specifically to screen for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, particularly 21-hydroxylase deficiency, in which this precursor accumulates.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DHEA-S helps localize excess to an adrenal versus ovarian source; it is not the CAH screen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Free testosterone confirms biochemical hyperandrogenism but does not identify CAH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LH helps assess the HPG axis but does not screen for an adrenal enzyme defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SHBG affects the free testosterone fraction and is not a screening test for CAH.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old competitive bodybuilder presents with 1 year of infertility. Examination shows marked muscularity, truncal acne, and small, soft testes bilaterally. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum testosterone with low LH and low FSH. Which of the following best explains his infertility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Androgen receptor insensitivity in peripheral target tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deficient aromatization of testosterone to estradiol in adipose tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exogenous androgen suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary testicular failure from prior mumps orchitis with tubular atrophy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolactin-mediated suppression of hypothalamic GnRH pulse release

explanation.summary: Exogenous androgens suppress the HPG axis, causing testicular atrophy and infertility despite high testosterone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exogenous androgen use is the most prevalent cause of androgen excess in young men. It suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary output, lowering LH and FSH, which produces testicular atrophy (loss of FSH support) and infertility even though circulating testosterone is elevated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Androgen insensitivity produces elevated testosterone with an elevated, not suppressed, LH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aromatase deficiency causes skeletal abnormalities from estrogen deficiency; it does not explain suppressed gonadotropins with atrophic testes in a steroid user.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary testicular failure would show low testosterone with elevated LH and FSH from loss of negative feedback.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperprolactinemia causes secondary hypogonadism with low testosterone, not elevated testosterone.

questions.stem: Laboratory evaluation of a patient with a disorder of androgen physiology shows an elevated serum testosterone together with an elevated LH. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Androgen insensitivity syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exogenous androgen use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone-secreting tumor

explanation.summary: Elevated testosterone with elevated LH indicates androgen insensitivity syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: When target tissues cannot respond to androgens, negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary fails, so LH stays high and continues to drive testosterone production. The combination of high testosterone and high LH is therefore the signature of androgen insensitivity syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Exogenous androgens raise testosterone but suppress LH through intact negative feedback.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary hypogonadism shows low testosterone with elevated LH from gonadal failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary hypogonadism shows low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal LH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A testosterone-secreting tumor also produces high testosterone with a suppressed LH.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated for absent pubertal development. He has small testes, no facial or axillary hair, and reports that he has never been able to smell. Serum testosterone, LH, and FSH are all low. Which of the following best explains his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 47,XXY karyotype with primary testicular failure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive deficiency of the aromatase enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failed migration of GnRH-producing neurons during fetal development

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ischemic testicular injury from remote testicular torsion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolactin-secreting tumor compressing the pituitary stalk

explanation.summary: Kallmann syndrome pairs hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia due to failed GnRH neuron migration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by impaired migration of GnRH-producing neurons during fetal development. Delayed or absent puberty with a reduced or absent sense of smell distinguishes it from other causes of secondary hypogonadism, and the low LH and FSH confirm the central defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Klinefelter syndrome is primary hypogonadism, so LH and FSH would be elevated, and anosmia is not a feature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aromatase deficiency presents with tall stature, unfused epiphyses, and osteoporosis with elevated testosterone and gonadotropins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testicular torsion causes primary testicular failure with elevated gonadotropins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperprolactinemia can cause secondary hypogonadism but does not explain lifelong anosmia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with confirmed symptomatic hypogonadism (two low morning testosterone levels with low LH and FSH) wishes to conceive a child with his partner within the next year. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gonadotropin therapy with hCG

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intramuscular testosterone replacement therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metformin for metabolic support

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spironolactone with dose titration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transdermal testosterone replacement therapy

explanation.summary: Men with hypogonadism who desire fertility should receive gonadotropin therapy, not testosterone replacement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Testosterone replacement therapy is contraindicated in men desiring fertility because it suppresses spermatogenesis. In these patients, gonadotropin therapy with hCG, with FSH added if needed, is preferred because it stimulates endogenous testosterone production and preserves fertility.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Intramuscular testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis and would undermine his fertility goal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin addresses insulin resistance in PCOS and has no role in treating male hypogonadism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spironolactone is an androgen receptor blocker used for hirsutism in females and would worsen androgen deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The route does not change the problem; transdermal testosterone also suppresses spermatogenesis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of a tender, firm subareolar mass of the left breast consistent with true gynecomastia. He takes no medications and does not use anabolic steroids. Serum estradiol is elevated. In addition to LH, FSH, and testosterone levels, which of the following is the most appropriate next step to exclude a dangerous underlying cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal CT with serum cortisol measurement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Core needle biopsy of the breast tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Empiric anastrozole with follow-up examination

choices.label: D
choices.text: MRI of the pituitary with prolactin level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum hCG and AFP with testicular ultrasound

explanation.summary: New gynecomastia with elevated estradiol in a young man requires hCG, AFP, and testicular ultrasound to exclude a germ cell tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: In males with gynecomastia, hCG, alpha-fetoprotein, and testicular ultrasound are obtained to exclude a germ cell tumor. Recognizing gynecomastia as a potential sign of an underlying tumor, such as a Leydig cell or germ cell tumor of the testis, is a key clinical skill, and this evaluation takes priority in a young man with unexplained estrogen excess.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal imaging is pursued when elevated DHEA-S or cortisol suggests adrenal pathology, which has not been shown here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Breast biopsy evaluates the local tissue but does not identify the underlying source of estrogen excess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aromatase inhibitors treat persistent hyperestrogenism only after the root cause has been identified and addressed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pituitary workup does not address the estrogen-secreting testicular tumors that must be excluded first in this setting.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man treated with spironolactone develops bilateral painful breast enlargement. Serum estradiol and testosterone are within normal limits. Which of the following best explains his gynecomastia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct stimulation of estrogen receptors by the drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: hCG secretion from an occult germ cell tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired hepatic metabolism of circulating estrogens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased estradiol synthesis by the adrenal glands

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased peripheral aromatization in adipose tissue

explanation.summary: Spironolactone causes gynecomastia by stimulating estrogen receptors, not by raising estrogen levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spironolactone does not increase estrogen levels; it causes an estrogen-like effect. It blocks aldosterone and androgen receptors and also stimulates estrogen receptors, producing painful breast enlargement in women and gynecomastia in men, which fits his normal estradiol level.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A germ cell tumor would be suggested by an elevated hCG and abnormal hormone levels, not normal labs on a culprit drug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Liver disease elevates estrogen levels by impairing their metabolism, which is not seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no indication of an adrenal source, and his estradiol is not elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Obesity-related aromatization raises estradiol, but his estradiol is normal.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with a BMI of 36 kg/m2 presents with vaginal bleeding 3 years after her last menstrual period. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined oral contraceptive pills for cycle control

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial biopsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassurance with routine annual follow-up

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum estradiol measurement repeated in 3 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transvaginal ultrasound deferred for 6 months

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding warrants urgent evaluation with endometrial biopsy for endometrial pathology.
explanation.whyCorrect: In postmenopausal women, any uterine bleeding warrants urgent evaluation for endometrial pathology, and endometrial biopsy is indicated for postmenopausal bleeding. Her obesity increases peripheral aromatization of androgens to estrogens, and chronic unopposed estrogen exposure raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: OCPs manage anovulatory bleeding in premenopausal women and would not evaluate for carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Postmenopausal bleeding is never reassured away; endometrial pathology must be excluded urgently.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Measuring estradiol delays the tissue diagnosis that postmenopausal bleeding requires.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deferring imaging for months delays evaluation of a finding that demands urgent workup.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had irregular menses for 5 months, followed by hot flashes and vaginal dryness. FSH is elevated on two measurements taken 6 weeks apart, and estradiol is low. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Annual FSH monitoring without additional testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endometrial biopsy of the uterine lining

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotype analysis and FMR1 premutation testing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metformin therapy for insulin resistance

explanation.summary: Confirmed primary ovarian insufficiency prompts testing for its causes, including karyotype and FMR1 premutation analysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: POI is diagnosed in women under 40 with menstrual irregularity for at least 3 consecutive months and two elevated FSH levels at least 1 month apart, which this patient meets. Once confirmed, testing for causes should include karyotype analysis, FMR1 gene testing for the fragile X premutation, adrenal antibodies, and screening for concurrent autoimmune disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Watchful waiting misses the etiologic workup and delays hormone therapy needed to protect bone and cardiovascular health.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endometrial biopsy evaluates suspected endometrial pathology from estrogen excess, not estrogen deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metformin treats insulin resistance in PCOS and has no role in primary ovarian insufficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her elevated FSH localizes the failure to the ovary; a low FSH would instead suggest a central hypothalamic or pituitary cause worth imaging.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is evaluated after a low-impact wrist fracture. He is 203 cm tall, and radiographs show open growth plates and markedly reduced bone density. Serum testosterone and androgen precursors are elevated, estradiol is undetectable, and LH and FSH are elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his skeletal disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aromatase inhibitor therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exogenous estrogen replacement therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gonadotropin therapy with hCG

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone replacement therapy

explanation.summary: In male aromatase deficiency, exogenous estradiol corrects the skeletal abnormalities and closes the epiphyses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elevated testosterone and androgen precursors with undetectable estradiol and elevated gonadotropins confirm aromatase deficiency. This condition demonstrates that estrogens, not androgens alone, are critical for bone health and epiphyseal closure in males, and exogenous estradiol replacement corrects the skeletal abnormalities and closes the epiphyses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An aromatase inhibitor would deepen the estrogen deficiency; these drugs are used to lower estrogen in hyperestrogenic males.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Supplementation does not address the estrogen deficiency driving his unfused epiphyses and osteoporosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: hCG stimulates endogenous testosterone production for hypogonadal men desiring fertility and does not supply the missing estrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: His testosterone is already elevated; androgens alone cannot close the epiphyses or restore bone density.
